analysis.one_liner: Stops credit card companies from raising rates on existing balances and piling on fees, and restricts marketing cards to young adults.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote, after being referred there the same day it was introduced in March 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped credit card companies from raising the interest rate on money you already owe, limited penalty rates to specific violations listed in your card contract (capped at 7 percentage points), and barred late fees when a payment was postmarked or sent electronically on time. It also would have capped fees at roughly what it actually costs the issuer, required companies to check that a new cardholder could afford the payments before issuing or expanding credit, and stopped credit bureaus from selling the names of 18-to-20-year-olds for pre-approved card offers unless they opted in. It was introduced by Senator Robert Menendez in March 2008, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a vote of any kind before the Congress ended [S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially those carrying balances. The bill would have protected balances already owed from rate hikes, limited penalty rates to violations the card contract actually spells out (and capped those at 7 percentage points), and stopped late fees when payment was mailed or sent electronically on time. It also would have shielded 18-to-20-year-olds from pre-screened card offers unless they opted in, and required issuers to check a borrower's income and obligations before issuing a card or raising a limit [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cardholders carrying balances, and young adults

how_it_helps.text: It banned retroactive rate increases: if a card's rate went up, the higher rate would apply only to new purchases, not to balances already owed [S2][S3].

It barred issuers from raising rates, fees, or finance charges before a card's scheduled renewal date, except for a disclosed introductory rate expiring, a disclosed variable rate, or a disclosed penalty [S2][S3].

It allowed penalty rate increases only for specific violations listed in the card contract, capped any penalty increase at 7 percentage points, and explicitly said a drop in the consumer's credit score could not be the reason [S2][S3].

It said a payment postmarked or sent electronically by the stated date could not trigger a late fee, a rate hike, or other penalties, and capped fees at roughly the issuer's actual cost of the violation [S2][S3].
It required issuers to verify, before opening an account or raising a credit limit, that the consumer could afford the scheduled payments based on income, obligations, and employment [S2][S3].

It stopped credit bureaus from selling 18-to-20-year-olds' names for pre-screened credit and insurance offers unless the young person affirmatively opted in, and required mailed credit offers to state the actual rate, fees, and credit limit instead of teaser terms [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks. They would have lost the ability to reprice existing balances at any time, to raise rates based on credit-score drops or unrelated information, and to charge late and penalty fees beyond their actual costs. Prescreened marketing to young adults would have become opt-in, shrinking a customer acquisition channel [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The ability-to-pay verification requirement could make it harder for young people, students, and people with little documented income to get a first credit card, since issuers would have to confirm expected income and employment before opening an account or raising a limit [S3].

Limiting penalty rate increases to 7 percentage points and capping fees at the issuer's actual cost removes a major way card issuers price for risk; issuers argued this would force them to charge higher rates to everyone up front or tighten lending across the board [S3].

The bill required regulators to write detailed formulas for determining ability to pay and cost-based fee caps, which critics could reasonably call rigid rules that a one-size-fits-all regulator would administer poorly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have been concrete and fell on ordinary households: no surprise rate hikes on old balances, no penalty rates triggered by an unrelated dip in a credit score, late fees only when a payment was genuinely late, and fewer pre-approved card offers aimed at 18-to-20-year-olds [S2][S3]. The costs were real but manageable: issuers argued that blocking "anytime" repricing removes their main tool for managing risk, so they might charge higher rates or fees up front or approve fewer borrowers, and an ability-to-pay rule could make it harder for students or people with thin credit files to get a card at all [S3]. On balance, similar restrictions were later adopted industry-wide, which suggests the consumer benefits outweighed the flexibility issuers gave up — but none of that mattered here, because the bill never advanced far enough for anyone to weigh the tradeoffs in the open [S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions were introduction on March 12, 2008 and referral the same day to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in the action history; the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill still in committee [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].

Its provisions — barring retroactive rate increases, restricting penalty pricing, limiting fees, and requiring ability-to-pay checks — closely resemble the credit card reforms Congress passed the following year, after this bill had already died [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept for another year the ability to raise rates on existing balances, charge penalty rates tied to credit scores, and collect fees above their costs. Cardholders kept paying for it.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Reform Act of 2008 on March 12, 2008.

for.name: Two Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 12, 2008 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Credit card issuers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on rate increases and fees during the 2008 credit card reform debate, in which issuers argued such rules would raise costs and restrict access to credit.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the Banking Committee never acted, so no record of partisan division exists.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and finance companies)
industries.note: The bill cut off several major revenue streams: raising rates on existing balances, penalty pricing triggered by credit-score drops, fees above the issuer's actual cost, and unilateral contract changes. These practices were core to how card companies priced risk and profit [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and prescreened credit-marketing firms
industries.note: Bureaus could no longer sell the names of 18-to-20-year-olds for pre-approved credit and insurance offers unless the consumer opted in, shrinking a marketing channel aimed at new borrowers [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Card issuers marketing to young consumers
industries.note: Requiring proof of ability to pay before issuing a card or raising a limit would have curtailed issuing credit to young customers without income, a segment issuers had pursued heavily [S3].
